question: Under Indian law, a child born during a valid marriage is presumed to be the legitimate child of the husband, and this presumption can be rebutted solely by the husband's sworn denial.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. The legitimacy presumption under Section 112 IEA requires proof of non-access to rebut — not merely a denial. Courts increasingly rely on DNA paternity testing to resolve disputes, but a bare denial by the husband cannot rebut the presumption of legitimacy.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. The presumption of legitimacy under Section 112 of the Indian Evidence Act is one of the strongest in law but can only be rebutted by proof of non-access (i.e., that the husband had no opportunity to be the father at the relevant time). A sworn denial by the husband alone is insufficient to rebut the presumption; DNA evidence may be required by a court.
